extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and journalists (newswire consumers and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Production of short-to-medium length newswire dispatches reporting international political, military, and domestic events (AP-style datelines, source attribution, leads, and background).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance/embargo release
rubrics_metrics.description: END ADVANCE FOR USE AT 12 NOON EASTERN TUESDAY JULY 1
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories may carry explicit embargo/advance instructions indicating a required release time. Editors and wire clients must observe the stated embargo ('advance for use at ...') and not publish before the indicated time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and agency attribution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each dispatch uses a dateline (city, date) and the wire service tag (AP). Use the dateline to show reporting location and date; include the agency abbreviation to indicate source/ownership of the copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source attribution language
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases used to attribute information to sources: 'THE COMPANY SAID', 'THE ARMY SAID', 'MRS. SUSANNA SHALLNA... TOLD A WORKSHOP GROUP', 'THE U.S. DELEGATE, ERNEST A. GROSS, INSISTED'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute factual claims and opinions to named sources or institutional voices rather than presenting them as reporter-established facts. Use clear verbs (said, told, insisted, announced) and identify the source's role where possible (e.g., 'the army', 'the company', named individuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling classified/sensitive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Text notes that 'MANY OF THE DETAILS OF THE NEW TANK'S CONSTRUCTION ARE STILL CLASSIFIED.' and 'DISCLOSURE OF THE FIRE DAMAGE HAD NOT BEEN MADE KNOWN BECAUSE OF SECURITY REGULATIONS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should note when details are classified or withheld for security reasons; avoid publishing information that would violate security restrictions. When possible, acknowledge the limitation explicitly in copy ('details ... are still classified').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead summarization of main facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Example lead material: opening paragraphs on 'THE PATTON 48 IS NOW...' summarizing production, contracts, delay from fire, crew complement and power plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a concise summary of the most important facts (what, who, where, when, why/how) in the lead paragraph(s) so readers immediately grasp the key points of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct quotes and extended quoted speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted passages and speeches appear (e.g., 'WE ARE UNALTERABLY OPPOSED TO MISINFORMED PERSONS SEEKING TO UNDERMINE...'; GROSS's 4,000-word speech quoted/described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include direct quotations for key statements, identify the speaker, and use quotations to convey tone and exact claims. For long speeches, summarize main thrusts and include brief representative quotes rather than reproducing entire lengthy addresses unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context, background and comparative detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories provide background and comparisons (e.g., T-43 weighing over 50 tons, 'comparable Russian heavies are the IS-4, weighing 52 tons'; historical/technical context about heavy tanks and bridge limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply relevant background, technical detail, and comparisons to help readers understand significance (historical precedents, technical specs, policy reasons). Place new facts in context rather than presenting them in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official documents and primary communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'telegrams signed by President Sarah T. Hughes...sent to Senators...', proposals asking the Red Cross to send a commission, and other telegrams/official requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on and cite primary official communications (telegrams, resolutions, proposals) when available; identify who authored/sent the documents and their recipients to strengthen sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story metadata and newsroom codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of editorial markers and codes such as 'GG849AED B26 (240)', 'JM655PED', story-length/priority numbers and section headings like 'NIGHT LEAD BUSINESS WOMEN', 'LEAD DAY U.N.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire copy often contains internal metadata (story IDs, length codes, priority tags, section labels). Maintain these markers for editorial workflow and to indicate intended placement/length; strip or convert them appropriately for publication if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple datelines/dispatches for different locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple location-tagged reports appear (e.g., 'UNITED NATIONS, JULY 1-CAP-', 'BOSTON, JULY 1-(AP)-', 'TOKYO, JULY 2-(AP)-', 'LONDON, JULY 2-(AP)-').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing a collection of dispatches, keep each piece's dateline and location tagging to preserve sourcing and situational context; ensure readers can distinguish separate dispatches and their origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral tone and attribution when reporting contentious claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting disputed or inflammatory allegations (e.g., 'COMMUNIST CHARGES OF GERM WARFARE'), the copy usually attributes claims and reports rebuttals (Soviet denial, calls for impartial investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For contested or serious allegations, present the claim as attributed, include responses or denials where possible, and note calls for independent verification (investigation commissions) rather than asserting unverified charges as fact.
